entries.title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). The shape of cluster haloes revealed by intracluster light
entries.summary: Intracluster light (ICL) offers a luminous route for measuring the shapes and orientations of cluster haloes. We used Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1) images to quantify ICL shapes for 205 clusters at $0.1 \leq z \leq 0.8$ selected from the eROSITA All-Sky Survey and the Dark Energy Survey. We measured the ICL properties across five bands ($I_\mathrm{E}$, $Y_\mathrm{E}$, $J_\mathrm{E}$, $H_\mathrm{E}$ and the coadded $YJH_\mathrm{E}$), and find that the shape parameters are consistent across the filters, with the $H_\mathrm{E}$ band probing the profiles to the largest cluster-centric distances ($0.1R_{200\mathrm{c}}\sim100$ kpc). The ICL ellipticity ($e=1-b/a$) distribution peaks at 0.5, consistent with halo ellipticities inferred from strong and weak lensing studies, suggesting that the ICL traces the large-scale structure of the clusters. Cluster cores, dominated by brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) light, are round ($e\sim0.2$), while the ICL becomes progressively more elongated at large radii, reaching an ellipticity of $\sim0.5$ by $0.1R_{200\mathrm{c}}$. We find that the ICL is closely aligned with the BCG (87% lie within 30$^\circ$), but shows a weaker alignment with the satellite galaxy distribution (61% within 30$^\circ$). Robust position angles could be measured using the ICL for 63% of the sample, whereas position angles could be measured for only 30% of the sample using the satellite galaxies. Stacking clusters in redshift bins allows measurements of the ICL surface brightness to $0.6$-$0.8R_{200\mathrm{c}}$ and ellipticity beyond $0.3$-$0.4R_{200\mathrm{c}}$ (300-400 kpc), but we observed a plateau in the ICL ellipticity beyond $0.1R_{200\mathrm{c}}$. These results demonstrate the capability of Euclid to characterise the ICL morphology with high statistical precision, allowing new constraints on cluster halo structure and its evolution with redshift.

entries.title: 20,000 Rotation Periods in Nearby Open Clusters and Moving Groups from ZTF and ASAS-SN
entries.summary: Open clusters provide uniquely powerful laboratories for studying stellar evolution because their members share a common age and chemical composition. Stellar rotation of low-mass GKM dwarfs in open clusters provides direct empirical constraints on magnetic braking, with implications for stellar interiors, magnetic activity, and star--planet interactions. However, existing cluster rotation samples are dominated by space-based observations, whose limited spatial coverage and short observing baselines can make it difficult to construct an unbiased sample. Long-baseline ground-based time-domain surveys therefore provide an important complement to space-based photometry. I present a catalog of $\sim$20,000 periodic photometric signals, including stellar rotations, eclipsing-binaries, and classical pulsators, measured from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae (ASAS-SN) for members of nearby open clusters and moving groups within 1.5 kpc. This catalog provides a new empirical foundation for studying the mass, chemical composition, and age dependence of stellar angular-momentum evolution and for testing models of magnetic braking across a broad range of stellar masses and evolutionary states.

entries.title: IMF-aware N-body forward modelling of membership selection functions for young open clusters
entries.summary: We present an IMF-aware N-body forward-modelling framework, in which the stellar initial mass function (IMF) is an explicit input, to quantify the membership selection functions of open clusters, namely completeness and contamination as functions of magnitude. Accurate derivation of the IMF requires correcting for these selection effects, which otherwise distort the inferred present-day mass function. Our framework simulates clusters with IMF slopes $α_2 = -2.7, -2.3, -1.9$, converts them into synthetic Gaia observations, adds mock field populations, and recovers members with HDBSCAN to mimic observational membership selection. Applying this framework to 35 young open clusters (ages $\lesssim100$ Myr, distances $\lesssim600$ pc), we find declining completeness towards the faint limit; older, more expanded, and more diffuse models have lower completeness and higher contamination. For a given cluster, models with flatter IMFs yield modestly but systematically lower global completeness and higher contamination, despite initial cluster masses calibrated to the same observed member count. These models undergo more stellar evolution mass loss and expand more, resulting in lower projected stellar densities; their lower completeness is consistent with more diffuse clusters being harder to separate from field stars. Corrections derived from a mismatched IMF largely recover the total star counts but leave a larger distortion in the shape of the present-day luminosity function than those derived with the correct IMF. Because membership recovery is tied to a cluster's structural evolution and the specific membership algorithm used, our findings emphasize that selection functions should be inferred jointly with the IMF rather than assumed in advance.

entries.title: $N$-body simulations of the open cluster M67 -- I: global cluster properties
entries.summary: The most recent Gaia data releases have seen the construction of many open cluster catalogues containing thousands of open clusters. Simulations of these clusters are needed in order to interpret observations, both existing and upcoming. M67 is an ideal open cluster to calibrate these simulations due to its advanced age and large, diverse binary populations. Moreover it is one of the most extensively observed open clusters with observations in several wavelengths. We aim to reproduce the global cluster properties of M67 with modern $N$-body simulations, as well as comparing its observed properties in the largest homogeneous open cluster catalogue with other available observations. We carry out several NBODY6++GPU simulations with varying initial conditions, including metallicity, half-mass radius, and the distribution of orbital binary parameters. Our models broadly reproduce the observed global properties of M67, and we are able to recreate the cluster's surface brightness profile, radial mass profile, and colour-magnitude diagram. Our favoured model indicates an initial half-mass radius of around 1.6 pc, although its total observable cluster mass may be too high. Further simulations are planned for a subsequent study, with a focus on recreating the present-day binary populations of M67.

entries.title: Atypical White Dwarfs in Open Clusters
entries.summary: Open clusters are powerful laboratories for investigating the formation and evolution of white dwarfs (WDs), as their well-constrained ages link WDs to their progenitor stars. This is particularly valuable for atypical WDs, including magnetic WDs and those with non-hydrogen-dominated spectra, whose origins can be difficult to disentangle in the field. We assemble the largest sample to date of atypical WDs in open clusters: eight non-magnetic WDs with helium-dominated spectra, five with featureless spectra, and five magnetic WDs showing hydrogen or helium lines. We find no significant difference between the initial--final mass relations of hydrogen- and helium-atmosphere WDs, nor robust spatial or kinematic differences. The strongest difference from the field is a deficit of non-DAs between $0.8$ and $1.0\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, where the field predicts $6.0^{+0.8}_{-0.7}$ WDs, yet none are observed, with a probability of only $0.37\%$. Massive magnetic WDs show a similar deficit: only one of 20 cluster WDs with $M_{\mathrm{WD}}\geq1.0\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ and $T_{\mathrm{eff}}\geq20{,}000\,{\rm K}$ is magnetic, compared with 10 of 16 in the field. Together, these deficits are consistent with an additional field population of massive merger remnants, particularly high-mass magnetic WDs and warm/hot DQs. Such objects may be underrepresented in clusters because young systems provide limited time for certain classes of delayed mergers, while older clusters lose members or dissolve; the field accumulates binary evolution products over Galactic timescales. Magnetic cluster WDs consistent with single-star evolution further suggest mass-dependent magnetic-field emergence, with fields appearing early in some massive WDs while young lower-mass WDs remain consistent with delayed emergence.

entries.title: A Multi-dimensional Analysis of the Open Clusters NGC 2423 and NGC 2482 with Gaia DR3
entries.summary: We present a homogeneous photometric, astrometric, and kinematic study of the Hyades-like open clusters NGC 2423 and NGC 2482 based on Gaia DR3 data. Cluster memberships are determined using the UPMASK algorithm in the multi-dimensional parameter space of (alpha, delta, parallax, mu_alpha cos(delta), mu_delta), with radial velocities incorporated when available. Gaussian modelling of the astrometric distributions yields mean trigonometric parallaxes of 1.060 +/- 0.035 mas and 0.735 +/- 0.061 mas, corresponding to astrometric distances of 944 +/- 31 pc and 1361 +/- 113 pc for NGC 2423 and NGC 2482, respectively. Fundamental parameters are derived through PARSEC isochrone fitting, resulting in ages of 1250 +/- 100 Myr and 445 +/- 50 Myr, observed distance moduli (m-M)_obs = 9.90 +/- 0.10 and 10.80 +/- 0.20 mag, and reddening values E(G_BP-G_RP) = 0.07 +/- 0.01 and 0.10 +/- 0.02 mag, equivalent to E(B-V) = 0.054 and 0.078. The corresponding photometric distances are 892 +/- 50 pc and 1311 +/- 146 pc. We further investigate the internal and global kinematics of both clusters using velocity-ellipsoid parameters, the convergent-point method, and action-angular-momentum diagnostics. The derived kinematic properties show that NGC 2482 closely matches the velocity-space characteristics of the Hyades stream, while NGC 2423 shares the characteristic rotational velocity and angular momentum of the Hyades-like population but is offset in its U component. Both clusters occupy the angular-momentum range associated in the literature with Hyades-like clusters and bar-related resonances, although this association is based on their present-day kinematics and action-space locations rather than a direct dynamical demonstration of resonance trapping.
